name: Reis-Bucklers corneal dystrophy
aliases: corneal dystrophy of Bowman layer type 1
corneal dystrophy of Bowman layer type I (CDB1)

reference.source: Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology / Cornea by Krachmer
clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant dystrophy of the Bowman layer and superficial stroma, presenting in childhood with painful recurrent erosions
Caused by mutations in the TGFBI gene, placing it within the same gene cluster as granular and lattice dystrophies
Slit-lamp examination shows confluent greyish geographic or ring-shaped opacities at the level of Bowman layer
The deposits are granular (hyaline) material staining red with Masson trichrome, distinguishing it from the curly-fibre Thiel-Behnke dystrophy
Recurrent erosions are typically frequent and severe early in life, later giving way to reduced vision from superficial scarring and surface irregularity
Corneal sensation may be reduced and the surface becomes progressively irregular, degrading vision
Management uses lubrication and erosion care, with phototherapeutic keratectomy or lamellar keratoplasty for scarring and visual loss
Deposits and erosions characteristically recur superficially after treatment, including within grafts
reference.pathophysiology: Reis-Bucklers corneal dystrophy is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the transforming growth factor beta-induced gene (TGFBI). Abnormal mutant protein accumulates as hyaline (granular) deposits that replace and disrupt the Bowman layer and superficial stroma. Destruction of the Bowman layer weakens epithelial adhesion, producing frequent painful erosions in early life, while progressive deposition and superficial scarring create an irregular, hazy surface that reduces vision over time. Because the deposits arise from an inherited protein abnormality, they tend to recur in the superficial cornea after surgical removal.
additionalDifferentials: Thiel-Behnke corneal dystrophy (honeycomb Bowman layer dystrophy)
Epithelial basement membrane dystrophy with recurrent erosions
Superficial stromal scarring from prior keratitis
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy showing geographic Bowman layer opacities
Histology with Masson trichrome staining of hyaline deposits
TGFBI genetic testing to confirm diagnosis and distinguish from Thiel-Behnke dystrophy
Electron microscopy to differentiate granular rod-like from curly-fibre deposits when needed
Anterior segment optical coherence tomography to assess depth of superficial deposits
Corneal topography to quantify surface irregularity before treatment
redFlags: Frequent severe erosions causing disabling pain in childhood
Non-healing epithelial defect with risk of secondary infection
Progressive superficial scarring and irregular astigmatism reducing vision
Rapid recurrence of deposits after phototherapeutic keratectomy or grafting
reference.prognosis: Painful recurrent erosions dominate early life and later diminish as superficial scarring reduces vision. Superficial procedures can improve the surface, but deposits and erosions commonly recur, sometimes requiring repeated intervention.
pitfalls: Confusing it with Thiel-Behnke dystrophy without histological or genetic confirmation
Attributing childhood erosions to trauma and missing the hereditary dystrophy
Assuming a single procedure is curative despite the tendency to recur
Overlooking reduced corneal sensation and its impact on healing
references: Cornea by Krachmer, Mannis and Holland
management: Manage the frequent painful erosions of early life with ocular lubricants, hyperosmotic drops and a bandage contact lens, adding topical antibiotic cover for epithelial defects
Phototherapeutic keratectomy or superficial keratectomy to ablate the hyaline Bowman-layer deposits and rehabilitate vision and surface regularity
Favour superficial ablative techniques over full-thickness keratoplasty, as the inherited protein deposits recur in the superficial cornea after removal
Analgesia and, where needed, autologous serum drops to promote healing of recurrent erosions and improve epithelial adhesion
Serial slit-lamp examination, anterior segment imaging and topography to monitor deposit progression and surface irregularity
Genetic counselling for autosomal dominant TGFBI disease with examination of first-degree relatives
Refer to a corneal subspecialist for surgical planning and management of recurrent deposits, which may require repeated intervention
